clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in GABRB3, which encodes the beta3 subunit of the inhibitory GABA-A receptor, the principal fast inhibitory neurotransmitter receptor in the brain
Phenotypes span from milder genetic generalised epilepsies, including childhood absence and febrile seizures, to severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
Seizure onset is often in infancy or early childhood, with multiple seizure types including absences, myoclonic, tonic, and epileptic spasms
The electroencephalogram may show generalised spike-wave, multifocal discharges, or hypsarrhythmia depending on severity
Impaired GABA-A receptor function reduces inhibitory tone, so agents that enhance GABAergic transmission are often part of the therapeutic strategy
GABRB3 lies within the chromosome 15q11-q13 region, and the gene is also implicated in the neurodevelopmental overlap of that locus
Developmental impairment and autistic features are common in the encephalopathic end of the spectrum
reference.pathophysiology: GABRB3 encodes the beta3 subunit of the GABA-A receptor, a ligand-gated chloride channel that mediates fast synaptic inhibition. Pathogenic variants impair receptor assembly, trafficking, or channel gating, reducing inhibitory chloride currents and shifting the cortical balance towards excitation. This loss of inhibitory tone lowers the seizure threshold and perturbs the developmental maturation of neural circuits, producing epilepsy that ranges from self-limited generalised syndromes to severe encephalopathy. Because the core deficit is reduced GABAergic inhibition, therapies that potentiate GABA-A receptor signalling are mechanistically rational.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic or genetic generalised epilepsy of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Epilepsy gene panel or whole-exome sequencing to confirm the GABRB3 variant
Electroencephalography to define generalised versus multifocal patterns
Brain magnetic resonance imaging to exclude structural causes
Chromosomal microarray if a 15q11-q13 copy number change is suspected
redFlags: Progression to epileptic spasms with hypsarrhythmia
Frequent drug-resistant seizures with developmental regression
reference.prognosis: Milder generalised phenotypes may be well controlled with a good developmental outcome, whereas the developmental and epileptic encephalopathy end carries drug-resistant seizures and significant intellectual disability.
pitfalls: Assuming a uniformly severe course when the phenotype can be mild and self-limited
Neglecting GABA-enhancing strategies given the underlying inhibitory deficit
Overlooking coexisting autistic and behavioural features that need support
Failing to consider 15q11-q13 disorders in the differential
